deep.reconstruction:
The page has two unrelated groups of notes. The heading, if correctly read as the Kingdom of Westphalia, dates the postal notes to 1808–1813. The star notes fit February 1806.

(A) Heading: 'Brieftaxe im Königreich Westfalen' (postal letter tariff in the Kingdom of Westphalia, the Napoleonic state 1807–1813 to which Göttingen belonged). This dates the upper half to c.1808–1813, later than the 1805 bundle label.

1. Distance table. There are three columns: Kilometer | Meilen | Centimes. The postage rises by 10 centimes per distance zone: 15 c. as the base rate, then 20, 30, …, 120 c. Gauss converts zone limits between kilometres and miles. The entries are:
- 9 km ↔ 1 mile
- 36 ↔ 4
- 72 ↔ 8
- 107 ↔ 12
- [160] ↔ 18 (km lost to damage; my reconstruction)
- [213] ↔ 24 (km lost to damage; my reconstruction)
- 285 ↔ 32
- 356 ↔ 40
- 445 ↔ 50
- 534 ↔ 60
- 623 ↔ 70
- 889 ↔ 100

The implied factor is km = 8.89 × miles, i.e. 1 Meile ≈ 8.889 km. This equals 1/12.5 of a meridian degree on the metric definition (1° = 10000/90 km = 111.11 km), i.e. 2 French lieues communes of 25 per degree. Some entries (534, 623, 445, 285) match a rounded factor of 8.9 rather than 8.889.

2. Weight scale. Gauss takes 1 Loth = 16 g:
- 8 g = 1/2 Loth → single ('einfach') rate, 1
- 12 g = 3/4 Loth → 1½ rates
- 16 g = 1 Loth → 2 rates
- General rule above one Loth: 16 + 5x grams = 1 + 5x/16 Loth → 2 + x/2 rates. Each further 5 g adds half a single rate.

Below this is an unclear note, 'oder 256 …', followed by a small table: 16 … 6 Loth; 24 … 7; 24 … 8; 32. Its meaning is uncertain. It may be a heavier-item scale; for x = 48, 16 + 5x = 256 g.

(B) Astronomy, continuing the previous page's chart of the orbit of Pallas from 2 Feb to 13 Mar 1806 (RA 68–78°, Dec 11–24°). The planet sign is probably Gauss's Pallas sign rather than Jupiter, since the positions fall on that chart. The positions are RA 70°44′, Dec 20°24′; then […]59′ with Dec 20°3′; then declinations 20°38′ and 20°42′. These look like successive positions of the planet.

'Neu bestimmte Sterne febr. 13' gives newly reduced comparison stars:
- magnitude 8: α = 69°5′, δ = 20°22½′
- magnitude 7.8: α = 70°3½′, δ = 20°18′, marked with the planet sign (the planet near this star)
- magnitude 8.9: α = 71°11½′, δ = 20°36½′

These are ordinary reduction notes for Pallas observations in February 1806.
errors: 8 miles × 8.889 km = 71.1 km, but Gauss writes 72 (he used 9 per mile here, or made a slip).

The conversion factor is used inconsistently. 534 (60 mi), 623 (70 mi), 445 (50 mi) and 285 (32 mi) correspond to 8.9 km/mile (exact values 533.3, 622.2, 444.4, 284.4). 889 (100 mi) and 107 (12 mi) correspond to 8.889. These are only rounding inconsistencies.
Taking 1 Loth = 16 g is an approximation; the Cologne/Hanoverian Loth is about 14.6 g. It is evidently a deliberate convenient value for the tariff.

results.what: Conversion table of postal distance zones between kilometres and German miles (1 Meile ≈ 8.89 km) for the Westphalian letter tariff
Weight-progression rule: 16+5x grams = 1+5x/16 Loth → 2 + x/2 single rates
Positions of Pallas and newly reduced comparison stars, 13 Feb 1806
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (his Pallas work is well known)

deep.surprise_reason: Personal notes on postal rates (unit conversions) and routine comparison-star positions for Pallas observations. There is no mathematical content beyond arithmetic. The only point of mild historical interest is the dating clue: the Westphalia heading implies 1808 or later.

checkable.asserts: With factor 8.9: 9,36,71,107,285,356,445,534,623,890. This matches most of Gauss's entries.

transcription_corrections: The heading is read here as 'Brieftaxe im Königreich Westfalen' (letter postage tariff), not 'Briefltaxe'.
Reconstructed from the conversion factor: the damaged km entries for 18 and 24 miles should be about 160 and 213.
The symbol read as ♃ (Jupiter) is very probably Gauss's sign for Pallas. The coordinates (RA ≈ 70°, Dec ≈ 20°) lie on the preceding page's Pallas track for Feb 1806.
'einfach' (single rate) is the header of the third column of the weight table, placed above the 1, 1½, 2 entries.
